core: working definition (attributed): the pulse is the wave of blood you can feel each time the heart beats — blood flow caused by the beating heart, detected where an artery runs close to the skin (OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills; MedlinePlus counts it as heartbeats per minute)
normal adult resting reference range ~60-100 beats per minute (attributed), with the honest note that well-trained athletes often rest in the 40s-60s and children's ranges differ by age
the sites named: radial (wrist — the most common routine site), carotid (neck), brachial (inner arm), femoral (groin), pedal / dorsalis pedis (top of foot) — each with one line
rate, rhythm, and strength — the three things a pulse tells you, each named with one line
bradycardia and tachycardia — slow and fast resting pulse (below 60 / above 100 beats per minute), stated factually and attributed
what changes it: exercise, emotion, illness, and medications — each named with one line
the honest framing: the pulse is the heart's telegram — a quick readout, not the whole story; a single number only means something against the person's own baseline and context
supporting: pulse counted in beats per minute; counting a full minute or 30 seconds × 2 is standard (MedlinePlus)
pulse assessment gives information about the heart's pumping and, in emergencies, whether the heart is pumping at all (MedlinePlus; OpenStax)
pulse characteristics: rate (beats per minute), rhythm (regular vs irregular), strength/volume (weak-thready to bounding) (OpenStax)

factors affecting pulse: exercise raises it, sleep lowers it, fear/anxiety raise it; fever, hyperthyroidism, lack of oxygen, and low blood volume raise it; some medications change it (OpenStax; MedlinePlus Vital Signs)
individual trends matter: a rate that is normal for the population can still be a change for a specific patient (OpenStax heart-rate section example: typical ~65 vs 96)

claims.claim: The pulse is the wave of blood you can feel each time the heart beats: blood flow caused by the beating heart can be detected wherever an artery runs close to the surface of the skin, and the pulse count in beats per minute equals the heart rate.

The normal resting pulse for adults is about 60 to 100 beats per minute; well-trained athletes often rest in the 40-60 range because their hearts pump more blood per beat, and children normally have faster resting rates that slow with age.

The pulse can be felt at named sites where arteries pass near the skin — radial (wrist), carotid (neck), brachial (inner arm), femoral (groin), and pedal/dorsalis pedis (top of foot) — and the radial site is the usual choice for routine adult checks.

Assessing the pulse yields three pieces of information: rate (beats per minute), rhythm (whether beats come evenly), and strength (the force or volume of each beat, from weak and thready to bounding).
A resting pulse slower than 60 beats per minute is called bradycardia and a resting pulse faster than 100 beats per minute is called tachycardia; both terms describe rate alone, not a diagnosis.

Pulse rate responds to everyday and clinical influences: exercise raises it and sleep lowers it; intense fear or anxiety raises it; fever, infection, dehydration, hyperthyroidism, and low oxygen can raise it; and some medications change heart rate.

A single pulse number is only meaningful against the person's own baseline: a rate that sits inside the population range can still be a real change for one patient, so the pulse is best read as a quick telegram about the heart, not the whole story.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What exactly the pulse measures — beats per minute vs the felt wave of blood
positions: MedlinePlus opens with 'The pulse is the number of heartbeats per minute.'
OpenStax describes the pulse as blood flow caused by the beating heart, detected where arteries run close to the skin.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson leads with the felt-wave definition (what you experience at the fingertips) and immediately connects it to the count (heartbeats per minute) — both sources agree the count equals heart rate, so the two framings are combined rather than opposed.

positions: MedlinePlus lists well-trained athletes at 40 to 60 beats per minute.
OpenStax says athletes and adolescents can rest as slow as 40 to 50 beats per minute.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says athletes 'often rest in the 40s to 60s' and explains why (stronger hearts pump more per beat) — a range that contains both sources without inventing precision.

positions: MedlinePlus says resting rates continually high (tachycardia) or below normal (bradycardia) should be discussed with a provider.
OpenStax defines the terms by the numbers (<60, >100) and notes athletes can naturally rest below 60.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the numeric definitions factually and adds the honest note that the label describes the rate, not a diagnosis — a trained athlete at 52 can be perfectly healthy, which both sources support.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The phase-4 generated draft ('Pulse is a foundational concept in Nursing & Allied Health Foundations...') contained no factual clinical content — no definition, no range, no sites — so nothing in it survived the rewrite.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic boilerplate draft with a source-verified lesson: working definition attributed to OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills and MedlinePlus; adult reference range 60-100 bpm attributed to MedlinePlus; athlete note (40s-60s) supported by both sources; sites verified against OpenStax; rate/rhythm/strength verified against OpenStax; bradycardia/tachycardia numeric definitions verified; factors (exercise, emotion, illness, medications) verified against OpenStax and MedlinePlus.
